title: Delhi High Court Seeks FSSAI Response on Non-Dairy Products Sold as Paneer
excerpt: A bench has given the Centre, FSSAI and Delhi government six weeks to reply to a plea for inspections and disclosure, but declined an interim festive-season enforcement drive.
body:
• The Delhi High Court has given the Centre, FSSAI, the Delhi government and the Commissioner of Food Safety six weeks to respond to a plea against non-dairy products being sold or served as paneer.
  • The court declined to order an interim festive-season enforcement drive; for now, nothing changes at shops or restaurants.
  • For consumers in India: the plea argues there is currently no practical way to tell, especially in restaurant dishes, whether paneer is dairy or an analogue — checking the ingredient label on packaged products is the only reliable test available today.
  • The petition does not seek a ban on lawful plant-based or analogue products, only action against passing them off as paneer without disclosure.

The Delhi High Court has sought responses from the Centre, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the Delhi government and the Commissioner of Food Safety on a public interest litigation alleging that non-dairy products are being sold and served as paneer without telling consumers. A division bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma directed the authorities to file their replies within six weeks, according to Bar and Bench.

What the Petition Asks For

The PIL, filed by law student Ridhima Singh and advocate Avlokiteshwar Padmapani Sidharth, asks the court to direct regular inspections, sampling and testing of paneer at manufacturing units, wholesale markets, distributors, retail outlets and food-service establishments. Counsel for the petitioners argued that a customer ordering paneer at a hotel or restaurant assumes the dish is a dairy product, and that an analogue can be a replicate that looks and tastes like paneer, with no disclosure and no way for the consumer to discover the substitution. The plea points to dishes such as paneer tikka, kadai paneer and paneer butter masala, where the ingredient is invisible once cooked.

The petitioners also cited enforcement already taken elsewhere: food safety authorities in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and Chhattisgarh have acted against analogue or non-dairy paneer, including a Punjab order prohibiting it for a specified period, Live Law reported. The plea further referred to a Delhi Food Safety Department action at Okhla Sabzi Mandi in August 2026 in which about 508 kg of suspected spurious paneer was destroyed.

The Legal Argument

Asked by the bench which statutory rights were violated, counsel referred to the Food Safety and Standards Regulations of 2011, which prescribe standards for food products and additives. Paneer is a standardised dairy product under that framework; an analogue replaces some or all milk constituents with non-milk ingredients. The petitioners argued that the nutritional profiles differ sharply — paneer is high in protein, while, they submitted, analogues are largely carbohydrate — and that undisclosed substitution misleads consumers about what they are eating and paying for. The plea seeks compliance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the rules framed under it, rather than new legislation.

"It can be a replicate. It looks and tastes like paneer. There is no disclosure or way of knowing or discovering."

— Counsel for the petitioners, Delhi High Court

What the Court Did — and Did Not Do

The bench issued notice but declined the petitioners' request for interim directions. Counsel had sought a sampling and enforcement drive ahead of the Navratri and Dussehra festive season, when paneer demand rises; the court passed no such order. That means the legal position in Delhi is unchanged for now: analogue products that are lawfully manufactured and properly labelled remain legal, and the case will turn on the replies filed over the next six weeks.

What This Means for Consumers

For shoppers in India, the practical takeaway is narrow but real. On packaged products, the ingredient list and product name are the only reliable check: a product that cannot legally call itself dairy paneer must declare its actual composition, and the plea is aimed at products and dishes where that disclosure never reaches the buyer. In restaurants and cloud kitchens, diners currently have no equivalent check, which is the gap the petition asks the court to close through disclosure duties on hotels, restaurants, caterers and food-delivery businesses. The petitioners have been explicit that they do not seek a blanket prohibition on lawful plant-based or dairy analogue products — only action against passing them off as paneer. The authorities' responses, due within six weeks, will show whether FSSAI and the Delhi government treat this as an enforcement problem under existing law or a labelling problem requiring new rules.
